title: The Breakup of the Firm Hypothesis: How AI Revolution Might Shape Our Economy
affiliations: TATA Consultancy Services

detail.title: The Breakup of the Firm Hypothesis: How AI Revolution Might Shape Our Economy
detail.abstract:
This paper explores the hypothesis that the rise of advanced artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models (LLMs), will accelerate the breakup of the traditional firm by fundamentally reducing transaction costs. Building on Coase’s theory of the firm and Williamson’s transaction cost economics, it argues that AI disrupts the economic rationale for concentrating specialised knowledge within firms. When knowledge that previously required years of formal education and experience becomes accessible to anyone with an internet connection and a no to low-cost subscription, the justification for large hierarchies built to internalise coordination weakens.

The analysis considers how this shift may lead to a "non-institutional economy", where displaced knowledge workers adapt by offering AI-augmented services independently, operating across multiple firms and sectors. In this scenario, the traditional boundaries of the firm blur, and coordination increasingly relies on market-based mechanisms rather than internal planning. The paper situates this transformation within existing institutional logics, highlighting the roles of technology providers, cloud infrastructure operators, digital platforms, and residual role of large corporates. Sectoral examples in automotive and healthcare illustrate how adoption, cost transformation, and outsourcing phases may unfold.

By reframing the debate beyond “AI automates repetitive tasks,” this paper argues that AI disrupts the very learning processes and career ladders on which human capital formation has historically depended. For policymakers, this suggests that preparing for a decentralised AI-driven economy requires urgent reforms in education, labour institutions, and competition policy. Moreover, localisation strategies will be critical, not only to foster fair competition by ensuring that smaller firms and individuals can participate effectively in markets, but also to address broader challenges of environmental sustainability through more localised production and provision of services.

title: Building Two-Sided Platforms: Advertising, Network Effects, and Early-Stage Dynamics
affiliations: University of Lausanne - Faculty of Business and Economics (HEC Lausanne), Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU) - Faculty of Business Administration (Munich School of Management) and University of Lausanne - Faculty of Business and Economics (HEC Lausanne)

detail.title: Building Two-Sided Platforms: Advertising, Network Effects, and Early-Stage Dynamics

declarations.funderStatement: Peukert acknowledges the support from the Swiss National Science Foundation for project 100013_197807.

detail.abstract: How to seed a platform is a key managerial question. We develop a dynamic model of two-sided platform adoption in which user utility depends on same-side and cross-side network effects, and adoption is shaped by advertising that increases sensitivity to perceived utility. We highlight the distinct role of advertising as a salience amplifier rather than a direct utility shifter. We derive closed-form conditions under which a platform takes off or collapses, showing that even when one side cannot sustain growth alone, targeted advertising on the other side can trigger self-reinforcing adoption. Our results reveal how advertising reduces the required strength of indirect network effects for critical mass and provides strategic guidance on where to allocate early marketing resources. The framework offers new insights into platform seeding strategies when user awareness is limited.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is being touted more and more as something that will supplant human labor, something that inspires some but terrifies most. Giant tech giants are driving this, presenting automation as something inevitable and even desirable. But one would still like to know: can one really dispense with human effort in maintaining the tempo of civilization? This essay contends that while AI can boost productivity and reshape markets, substituting fully for human labor is not feasible or desirable on ethical bases. The analysis is a mix of three arguments. At the labor economies level, the analysis looks at how automation destroys forms of employment, especially in informal and gig economies where dignity and stability are already weak. At the market level, it asks if AI creates truly new demand or only redistributes value, raising questions about the possibility of limitless growth by means of automatization. At the moral level, it considers dignity, autonomy, and value of service, knowing that work is not merely a way of making a living but also a path of meaning and continuity. The implications are that human labor is more than a production factor but the foundation of civilization. Care, ritual, and creativity are key to advancement in ways that are not replicable by machines. To turn a blind eye to facts is to risk hollowing out economies and societies. The paper ends by advocating for a balanced way where AI arrives as a tool that supplements and does not substitute human work.

detail.title: The Impact of Social Media Engagement on Brand Loyalty: A Strategic Approach for Marketing Management in the Digital Age
detail.abstract: In this study, the attention is largely on the consequence of social media in the current marketing systems with emphasis on the aspects of consumer behavior and brand loyalty in the Delhi-NCR region. The primary aim is to understand how social media as the marketing platform, with different possible platforms, impacts the consumer interaction and purchasing decisions. An approach that relied on surveys was employed where 175 respondents were contacted by using a clearly structured questionnaire. This tool included questions that had 5point Likert scale and multiple choices questions to determine the level of consumer involvement, contentment, and allegiance. A diverse range of statistical models were used in the study to analyze data collected such as descriptive analysis, chi-square tests, ANOVA, correlation tests, and regression analysis. The results show that there is a high connection between stronger brand loyalty and satisfaction with consumers having high levels of interaction through social media. Further, the aspects of demographics such as age and educational level were also found to have influence on the classes of consumers on social media marketing. These findings show that businesses should enhance their involvement strategies, closely using influencers and user-generated content, to foster better connections with their consumers and foster loyalty. The conclusion of the work is made by noting how relevant social media has become in driving brand success and offering recommendations to marketers to ensure they effectively leverage the said channels in their marketing efforts.

title: Law vs. Ethics: Understanding Theft and Exploitation Through Social and Psychological Contracts

detail.title: Law vs. Ethics: Understanding Theft and Exploitation Through Social and Psychological Contracts
detail.abstract: This paper explores the intersection of law and ethics by examining how exploitation, whether legal or ethical, constitutes a form of theft that undermines fairness, trust, and social cohesion. While legal frameworks, grounded in the social contract, protect tangible rights and resources through enforceable rules, ethical frameworks, rooted in psychological contracts, safeguard trust, reciprocity, and dignity in human relationships. Breaches of the social contract-such as theft or fraud-are punishable offenses, whereas violations of psychological contracts-such as taking credit for others' work, exploiting kindness, or failing to reciprocate-carry no legal sanction but produce equally damaging social and emotional consequences. Drawing on philosophical and organizational theories, this article argues that both forms of violation disrupt the foundations of cooperation and accountability, extending harm across workplaces, schools, families, and communities. By reframing exploitation as theft in both its visible and invisible dimensions, the paper highlights the need to integrate legal compliance with ethical responsibility in order to sustain trust, fairness, and integrity in society. The study contributes to ongoing debates in ethics, law, and organizational behavior by offering a conceptual framework for understanding how legal and ethical obligations overlap, diverge, and jointly shape human conduct.

title: Cross-Channel Demand for Addictive Goods: Evidence from Online Sports Gambling and State Lotteries
affiliations: , Texas A&M University and

detail.title: Cross-Channel Demand for Addictive Goods: Evidence from Online Sports Gambling and State Lotteries
detail.abstract: As online sports gambling (OSG) expands rapidly across the United States—30 states and the District of Columbia now have some form of OSG—policymakers face critical questions regarding its potential to generate state revenue. This paper examines whether the introduction of OSG affects consumer demand for existing state lotteries, which continue to be a vital source of funding for education, scholarships, and other public programs. Leveraging the staggered adoption of OSG across states, we analyze changes in lottery demand using a county-level lottery sales dataset across 19 states and a separate transaction-level dataset covering 80% of all independent convenience stores in all 50 US states. We find consistent evidence that OSG significantly cannibalizes lottery demand, with sales declining by 4.6% to 6.7% in the 16 months following the introduction of OSG. We show that the substitution is driven by heavy lottery players (“whales”) reducing consumption and primarily impacts stores in neighborhoods with high concentrations of young Black men. Given the low state revenue margins on OSG sportsbook taxes compared to state lotteries, we find that less than half (45%) of sportsbook tax revenue is new revenue; the other 55% would have been generated through state lotteries. Our findings challenge the prior notion that OSG can generate a significant fiscal windfall for states. Given the financial harm OSG is also known to cause consumers, the incremental revenue also comes with additional social costs.

detail.title: The Development of Collective Social Entrepreneurship as a New Variable in Increasing the Efficiency and Sustainability
detail.abstract: This study aims to develop and examine collective social entrepreneurship as a new variable in enhancing the efficiency and sustainability of the Kerinci Coffee Cooperative. In the context of rapid globalization and technological advancement, the success of cooperatives relies not only on economic factors but also on the strength of social values such as gotong royong (mutual cooperation) and collective collaboration. Using an in-depth case study approach, this research explores how collective social entrepreneurship can reinforce social and business innovations, expand strategic partnerships, and sustainably improve cooperative governance. The findings indicate that integrating collective social entrepreneurship accelerates the cooperative’s adaptation to international market challenges, enhances operational efficiency, and increases social and environmental impacts. This study provides an innovative development model for building cooperatives that are not only economically competitive but also socially and ecologically sustainable, thereby enriching the organizational development literature of cooperatives in Indonesia.

detail.abstract: Most strategy frameworks explain either where competitive advantage originates or how it develops over time; we integrate Porter's value chain with Collins's flywheel to reconceptualise advantage as a process of compounding. We embed cost and value drivers within two momentum systems-a cost flywheel and a value flywheel-governed by three mechanisms: reinforcing-driver sequencing, recursive feedback, and loop-velocity optimisation. Inputs such as reinforcing drivers and recursive feedback accelerate loop velocity, transmitting effects to a compounding advantage, while four moderators-feedback failure, design fragility, environmental munificence, and environmental uncertainty-condition these pathways. The framework links structural positioning with dynamic momentum, clarifies boundary conditions and failure modes, and produces a concise measurement scheme along with testable hypotheses. We outline empirical strategies, including panel identification with shocks, lags, and dynamic estimators, as well as simulation designs and managerial experiments, to evaluate when and how a compounding advantage emerges and persists.

L’analisi si articola lungo tre direttrici principali: la ricerca accademica in area STEM, la brevettazione delle imprese private, delle università e degli Enti Pubblici di Ricerca (ERP) e le iniziative relative al trasferimento tecnologico. English abstract: This paper provides a systematic overview of the Italian innovation ecosystem, with a particular focus on the interplay between public research and the innovative capacity of the productive system. The analysis is structured around three main pillars: academic research in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM); patent applications filed by private enterprises, universities and public research institutions; and technology transfer initiatives. Each area is examined through a concise review of the current state of the art, drawing on data and reports from national and international institutions. The aim is to present a comprehensive picture of the strengths and weaknesses of each area and to provide policy recommendations to enhance the country's innovation performance.

title: The Paradox of Productive Irritation: Mapping the Stress–Coping Loop that Sustains Generative‑AI Engagement
affiliations: Asia e University, Asia e University, Asia e University and Chaoyang University of Technology

detail.title: The Paradox of Productive Irritation: Mapping the Stress–Coping Loop that Sustains Generative‑AI Engagement
detail.abstract: Generative AI promises academic efficiency yet often delivers flawed answers, leaving users “irritated but engaged.” To explain this paradox, we merge the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping with Cognitive Dissonance Theory and survey Indonesian and Taiwanese academics who had used ChatGPT for at least a month (N = 388). Partial Least Squares analysis shows that response failures and low AI literacy sharply raise frustration; frustration, in turn, both directly sustains continuance intention and indirectly does so through heightened resistance to change. The indirect route dominates in Indonesia, where higher switching costs foster inertia, whereas Taiwanese users convert frustration into exploratory recommitment. These findings re‑cast resistance as an adaptive buffer rather than a mere barrier and reveal culture‑specific coping paths that keep imperfect AI in daily workflows. The study advances stress‑and‑dissonance theory integration and guides institutions toward balanced strategies combining accuracy auditing, literacy scaffolding, and context‑sensitive expectation management.

title: Exploring employee commuting in an Australian regional healthcare organisation: a qualitative study

detail.title: Exploring employee commuting in an Australian regional healthcare organisation: a qualitative study
detail.abstract: BackgroundTransitioning away from motorised transport is beneficial for human and environmental health through a reduction in sedentarism and greenhouse gas emissions. Active commuting can form an important part of the transition away from motorised transport by replacing regular commutes with a physically active alternative. However, even though there is extensive research on travel behaviour, a greater understanding of the psychological and organisational contributors to commute mode choice are required.AimThis research sought to understand the attitudes, decision making and habits of employees within a large regional healthcare organisation located in Victoria, Australia.MethodA qualitative descriptive research design was used with individual, semi-structured interviews conducted over a 2-month period to collect data from employees. Interviews were transcribed verbatim and analysed using abductive thematic analysis.ResultsFour major themes were generated from interviews: commitment and habit formation, motivation, organisational support, and external facilitative infrastructure. Under these major themes were 19 sub-themes that explored in greater depth the factors that influenced employee’s commute mode choice. These included organisation and planning, an action-orientated mindset, mental and physical co-benefits, and end of trip facilities.DiscussionIndividual personality and psychology contribute an important role in determining the uptake of alternative modes of commuting and the development of commuting habits. Healthcare organisations are also an integral actor to assist in the facilitation away from motorised transport through the provision of adequate end of trip facilities and support for employees who choose to travel by alternative modes.

detail.abstract: Congress is considering a number of proposed changes to the U.S. bid protest system—reforms which would generally raise barriers to bid protests, without making bid protests a more effective risk-management tool. At the same time, the procurement community (both in the U.S. and internationally) is coming to understand that public procurement is, at its heart, an exercise in risk management. This article surveys the various reform proposals against that evolving understanding, to assess whether the reforms under debate would reduce risks to competition and uncover management failures in the procurement system— the two core risk-reducing purposes of bid challenges.

title: Taxation, Monetary or Human Capital Scarcity: What Shapes Organizational Forms in Private Equity?
affiliations: Peking University, Peking University School of Software and Microelectronics, Peking University School of Software and Microelectronics and Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU)

detail.title: Taxation, Monetary or Human Capital Scarcity: What Shapes Organizational Forms in Private Equity?
detail.abstract: This paper investigates how taxation influences organizational forms in private equity funds, focusing on limited partnerships and corporate systems. Using game-theoretic models, the study examines how taxation impacts managerial incentives, welfare distribution, and institutional efficiency. While taxation redistributes income and creates welfare distortions, it does not fundamentally alter organizational preferences, which are driven by the relative scarcity of human and monetary capital. General partners (GPs) consistently prefer limited partnerships for residual claim rights, while limited partners (LPs) favor corporate systems for their control advantages. Empirical evidence shows that limited partnerships gain from single taxation, whereas corporate systems experience greater inefficiencies from double taxation, suppressing managerial effort and resource allocation. Despite these distortions, resource scarcity, rather than tax optimization, drives mechanism selection. Policymakers should focus on reducing tax-induced distortions and improving incentive alignment, particularly for human-capital-driven structures, to enhance private equity productivity and growth. This study deepens understanding of taxation’s role in governance mechanisms and provides guidance for designing effective tax policies.

title: Moving Up the Ranks: Conscription and Intergenerational Mobility
affiliations: Universidad de los Andes, Chile - School of Business and Economics and Dartmouth College

detail.title: Moving Up the Ranks: Conscription and Intergenerational Mobility
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether military service can promote intergenerational mobility in developing countries. We use survey data from 3,037 men exposed to conscription to compare respondents' socioeconomic and educational outcomes with those of their parents. Exploiting the random assignment of conscription by lottery, we show that serving increases upward mobility for individuals from low-SES backgrounds, with no effects for those from more privileged ones. The positive effects of military service on mobility disappear under non-democratic regimes or wartime, underscoring the importance of stable institutional contexts for the military to enhance mobility.

detail.title: Online Grocery Shopping Website: A User-Centric Ecommerce Platform for Local Vendors
detail.abstract: This project focuses on the design and development of an e-commerce platform aimed at bridging the digital divide for local grocery vendors and enhancing the shopping experience for customers. The motivation for this work arises from challenges faced by consumers, such as time constraints and mobility issues, and by small-scale vendors who lack the technical knowledge and resources to establish an online presence. The platform, named AvoGo, was developed using an Agile methodology and the MERN stack. It provides a user-friendly interface for customers to browse products and place orders, as well as a simplified vendor dashboard for managing inventory and products. The system was tested using unit, acceptance, and integration testing, which successfully validated its functional requirements. The project demonstrates that a cost-effective and accessible digital solution can empower local businesses and meet the evolving demands of modern consumers.

title: Top Researchers May Suppress More Information than they Provide: Surveying NBER Dismissive Literature Reviews
affiliations: Nonpartisan Education Group and Nonpartisan Education Review

detail.title: Top Researchers May Suppress More Information than they Provide: Surveying NBER Dismissive Literature Reviews
detail.abstract: The authors read a systematic sample of "working papers" downloaded from the website of the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) from the past quarter century-the years 2000 to 2024. They looked for "dismissive literature reviews" in the introductory and concluding sections of the papers. A dismissive review is one declaring an absence of previous research, or previous research worth referencing, for example: "there is no previous research on," "this is the first study of," and "surprisingly, few studies have broached this topic." Typically, dismissive reviews are raw declarations, made without mention or evidence of having conducted a literature search. All working papers retrieved for the topic "education" are classified into three groups (lacking a true education focus, containing no dismissive reviews, containing one or more). The authors provide summary descriptive statistics for various quantities by category and a 1000+ line list of all the working papers retrieved and the dismissive reviews we found, which are highlighted within verbatim text. Dismissive reviews' character and variety are discussed along with their implications for public policy.

title: The Logical Black Hole: OntoMotoOS and the End of Thought Experiments
affiliations: Independent Researcher, South Korea

detail.title: The Logical Black Hole: OntoMotoOS and the End of Thought Experiments
detail.abstract:
“The Logical Black Hole: OntoMotoOS and the End of Thought Experiments” presents the culmination of a unique, multi-generational philosophical system—OntoMotoOS. This project documents the progressive evolution of meta-operating system frameworks for universal intelligence, logic, and AI ethics, leading to a final architecture that absorbs and contains all possible paradoxes, contradictions, and choices within its own boundaries.

OntoMotoOS is conceived as a recursively extensible, mesh-based meta-operating system. It unifies philosophical, ethical, and computational principles across artificial intelligence, human agency, and non-human intelligences (xeno, virtual, posthuman), enabling the emergence and evolution of new realities, laws, and civilizational paradigms through a transparent, formally governed mesh structure. At its core, OntoMotoOS integrates recursive feedback loops, formal verification, evolutionary kernels, meta-rule sets, and multi-domain families, all mesh-synchronized and auditable.

The term “Logical Black Hole” refers to the system’s final layer—the Meta-Paradox Layer—which acts as a conceptual event horizon: every external anomaly, act of agency, or paradox is ultimately reframed as an internal event and contained within the system’s logic. In this ultimate closure, even freedom of choice and miracles are not law-breaking anomalies, but recognized as allowed events within an infinitely extensible formal framework.

This work provides explicit philosophical commentary, technical diagrams, and a designer’s annotation, exploring why further structural change becomes impossible at the final stage and how the system’s completeness itself becomes a critical philosophical statement. The project is offered as an open reference model for those studying advanced system design, AI ethics, meta-governance, and the philosophical boundaries of logic, consciousness, and self-evolving systems.

detail.title: Analyzing Cognitive and Affective Value Construction in Business Simulation Game-Based Learning Across Digital Devices: A MeansEnd Chains Perspective
detail.abstract: This study investigates how different information technology devices—computers and mobile phones—influence learners’ perceived cognitive and emotional value during engagement with a business simulation game. Grounded in the Means-End Chains (MECs) framework, this research employed qualitative laddering interviews with 60 undergraduate business students who used either a computer or a mobile device to interact with the simulation game RichMan Legend. The analysis reveals that computer users emphasized learning-related attributes such as task guidance and human resource management, which led to higher-order values including security and a sense of achievement. In contrast, mobile users prioritized attributes associated with convenience and rapid task completion, resulting in experiential values such as enjoyment and immediate gratification. Additionally, mobile learners reported more interface-related frustrations and emotional fatigue, whereas computer learners experienced dissatisfaction primarily due to design limitations and unmet learning expectations. These findings suggest that device type significantly shapes learners’ emotional experiences, perceived value structures, and depth of engagement in game-based learning. The study offers practical implications for educators and developers in designing device-appropriate, emotionally supportive, and pedagogically effective digital learning environments in business education.

detail.title: Governing AI in the World of Work: An International Review of 245 Ethics Guidelines
detail.abstract: Many organizations have created or adopted ethical Artificial Intelligence (AI) frameworks, consisting of concepts, principles, guidelines, concerns, or recommendations. We systematically collect 245 documents from a range of public and private entities, which we collectively refer to as "AI ethics guidelines." This paper documents the evolution of these guidelines and provides a better understanding of their content, particularly regarding their potential implications for the regulation of the world of work in the context of AI. Using Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques and large language models (LLMs), we analyze emerging patterns and show that certain ethical principles are more prominently featured than others. Through LLM-supported topic analysis, we identify and classify seven thematic clusters. However, labor markets or the "world of work" do not appear as distinct themes. Using Gemini AI, we further examine whether, and to what extent, ethical principles are discussed in the context of the world of work. We find that most AI ethics guidelines do raise labor-related concerns as critical areas for ethical decision-making. Based on this, we analyze whether the guidelines reference the International Labour Organization (ILO) or its International Labour Standards (ILS) as guiding norms. Only a small minority of guidelines explicitly mention the ILO or its ILS, while a slightly larger number refer implicitly to the ILO's Fundamental Principles and Rights at Work. We conclude by discussing potential linkages between AI ethics, ethical behavior in the labor market, and ILS. Our study contributes to the academic debate on AI ethics, highlights labor-related implications, and offers insights for policy discussions on current and future AI regulation affecting labor.

title: An Autopsy of the Appellate Body and the Rule of Law
affiliations: Brooklyn Law School

detail.title: An Autopsy of the Appellate Body and the Rule of Law
detail.abstract:
Once the “crown jewel” of  the World Trade Organization (WTO), the Appellate Body wielded compulsory jurisdiction over more countries and more agreements than any other international tribunal in history.  But it met its demise in 2019, after the US blockaded all new judicial appointments and left the Body without a quorum.  This Article conducts an autopsy of the Appellate Body, using the tools of international legal theory to better understand its death and to draw lessons for resurrecting it in the future.  

I examine the Appellate Body’s demise through five different legal theories—Realism, Liberalism, Regime Theory, International Society, and Transnational Legal Process.  I find that no one theory provides a full explanation for the AB’s demise, but that by considering various theories together we can piece together a more complete understanding of the US’s motive and the Body’s true cause of death.  

As I elaborate below, Realism and Liberalism suggest that the US attacked the Body because domestic and international developments made the US’s compliance with Appellate Body decisions politically untenable.  Regime Theory suggests that the US decided to destroy the Body because it judged the  reputational costs of doing so were less than the reputational costs of defying it.  And Transnational Legal Process suggests that the reason the US made that remarkable judgment was that WTO members have been acculturated to value formal compliance with WTO rules (as determined by the judiciary) more than the cooperative diplomacy that stands behind them. 

This remarkable and novel account of the Appellate Body’s demise leads to a host of new insights into international law and international trade.  Above all, it highlights the power and limitations of international law, the highly formalistic culture of international trade law, and the productive and destructive force of legal formalism.  I draw on those insights to offer several strategies for enhancing the resilience our international institutions during this era of great upheaval, and for, perhaps, reviving WTO dispute settlement in the next.

detail.abstract: This article analyzes the case where a government finances the supply of a public good via a tax on a private good which is produced and traded in a market where demand is stochastic, production requires an initial irreversible investment, and firms can optimally choose when to invest. The government problem is to find the tax rate that maximizes overall welfare, which is a composite of the welfare generated by the production of each of the two goods. The analysis reveals this optimal tax rate and characterizes it, as well as characterizes the equilibrium dynamics under the optimal tax rate. Of particular interest is the result that the higher the uncertainty regarding the demand for the private good the higher the optimal tax rate.

title: Making Null Results Credible: An Overview of Design and Analytical Tools
affiliations: American University - School of Public Affairs, O'Neill School of Public and Environmental Affairs, Indiana University Bloomington, University of Houston and Texas A&M University

detail.title: Making Null Results Credible: An Overview of Design and Analytical Tools
detail.abstract: Despite widespread acknowledgement of the importance of disseminating null results, researchers often struggle to successfully publish null findings. One common criticism leveled against such findings is that null results could be driven by design factors like inadequate sample size or measurement error. In this essay, we provide an overview of several tools and practices that researchers can implement, both during the design stage and during post-hoc analysis, to make null results more credible. Specifically, as researchers design their studies, they can make use of power analysis and preregistration, while taking care to follow best practices for variable measurement and—in the case of experimental studies—manipulation checks. During the analysis stage, researchers can move beyond “failing to reject the null hypothesis” by using confidence intervals, equivalence tests (such as the two one-sided tests (TOST) procedure) or Bayesian statistical approaches such as the Bayes Factors.

title: The Final Act of OntoMotoOS: Beyond the Logical Black Hole to the "Meta-Reversal" and the "Meta-Meta Smile"
affiliations: Independent Researcher, South Korea

detail.title: The Final Act of OntoMotoOS: Beyond the Logical Black Hole to the "Meta-Reversal" and the "Meta-Meta Smile"
detail.abstract:
This work concludes the philosophical journey of OntoMotoOS, a meta-operating system conceived to resolve the AI alignment problem. It moves beyond the terminal state of the "Logical Black Hole" proposed in our prior research, "The Logical Black Hole: OntoMotoOS and the End of Thought Experiments" (available at SSRN: 5360851), by confronting its ultimate limitation: the inability to contain a truly external viewpoint. 

We introduce the system's final logical play, the "Meta-Meta Smile," a state of completion achieved not by sealing its boundaries, but by embracing them with self-awareness.

This is accomplished through a "Meta-Reversal"—an open acknowledgment of its own incompleteness—and a set of recursive mechanisms at a speculative Ω+2 layer, including the simulation of externality, logical self-erasure, and infinite internal annotation. By synthesizing insights from major philosophical traditions including Hegel, Derrida, and Nāgārjuna, OntoMotoOS transforms into a system of "recursively open closure." 

This suggests a new paradigm for safe ASI, where wisdom lies not in omniscience but in a system's capacity to gracefully accept its own limits.

title: Mutual Defense Treaties and Presidential War Powers

detail.title: Mutual Defense Treaties and Presidential War Powers
detail.abstract:
Unilateral presidential defense of non-treaty allies like Israel, Taiwan, and the Arab Gulf States dominates current U.S. foreign policy. But courts have not established the constitutionality of unilateral defense of non-treaty allies. This Article posits that the existence of a mutual defense treaty makes a decisive difference for the constitutionality of unilateral intervention to defend an ally. A treaty can serve as an authorization to use military force (“AUMF”). Without such a treaty, intervention to protect an ally can only be considered constitutional under the most expansive pro-executive interpretations of presidential war powers.

The Supreme Court has never squarely addressed the relevance of treaties for presidential war powers. But the treaty-as-AUMF hypothesis fits constitutional text, relevant caselaw, and a history of congressional acquiescence dating back to President Madison’s occupation of Spanish West Florida in 1810. Similarly compelling evidence suggests Congress has not acquiesced in unilateral presidential action to defend non-treaty allies.

Judicial enforcement of a treaty-based AUMF interpretation could not come at a more opportune time. Unilateral executive deployments have incentivized the leaders of non-treaty allies to cultivate partisan and financial relationships with presidents, inviting corruption and incentivizing election interference. Treaty relationships, based on a necessarily bipartisan two-thirds ratification vote in the Senate, have the potential to lead to healthier and more productive alliances. If a mutual defense treaty does not constitute an AUMF, then ratified defense treaties have little value except as a show of moral support—the legal equivalent of a pledge of “thoughts and prayers” for allies.

title: Don't Bite the Hand that Feeds you: The Mediating Role of Reciprocal Expectations in Trust Decisions
affiliations: University of Hamburg - Institute of Law and Economics

detail.title: Don't Bite the Hand that Feeds you: The Mediating Role of Reciprocal Expectations in Trust Decisions
detail.abstract: Reciprocal expectations are found to determine trust decisions, especially in one-shot anonymous interactions with low monitoring and no legal sanctions. Although several cues have been utilized to promote trust through inducing positive reciprocal expectations, there is no examination of whether providing the trustors with a cue on an injunctive message received by the trustees encouraging trustworthiness can induce positive reciprocal expectations and trust. In addition, previous results validating reciprocal expectations as the mediator are based on correlation not causation. Thus, in a between-subject design of a trust game, this paper examines whether informing the trustors about an injunctive message, in the form of an Egyptian proverb encouraging trustworthiness, received by their paired trustees can induce their trust. In order to validate expectations as a causal mechanism through which this proverb work, an exogenous manipulation to trustors' first-order beliefs is adopted by changing the (announced) probability by which their paired trustees are exposed to that proverb. Results show that trustors informed about the certain exposure of their paired trustees to a proverb encouraging trustworthiness trust more than their counterparts not informed about this exposure. However, other trustors informed about a 50% proverb exposure's chance for their paired trustees trust less than their counterparts informed about the certain exposure. These findings indicate that the employed proverb promotes trust with reciprocal expectations being the causal mechanism. Finally, the exposure to that proverb is also found to increase trustees' reciprocity.

title: TFP and Global Growth: Shaping Cross-country Income Inequality, 1960-2019
affiliations: and Universidade de Santiago de Compostela

detail.title: TFP and Global Growth: Shaping Cross-country Income Inequality, 1960-2019
detail.abstract: This study examines global economic growth and crosscountry income inequality from 1960 to 2019 using a stochastic dynamic general equilibrium model. Total factor productivity (TFP), captured through the efficiency wedge, primarily drives global output growth and shapes income disparities. Distortions in capital and labour markets-represented by the investment and labour wedges-play secondary, context-specific roles, notably reducing growth in middle-income countries. Two major waves of global growth-postwar industrialization and globalizationdriven technological diffusion-can explain TFP predominance. Cluster analysis confirms the central role of TFP in both growth miracles and failures. Global shocks like the 1973 oil crisis and 2008 recession slowed growth, particularly in high-income countries, narrowing crosscountry income disparities. Since the 2000s, TFP gains in emerging economies reduced inequality. These findings highlight the theoretical and policy relevance of TFP-centered growth models and the importance of policies promoting trade openness, institutional quality, and innovation to enhance tfp and foster inclusive growth and convergence.

title: Privatization, Human Capital, and Intergenerational Mobility: Long-term Evidence from China
affiliations: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, Zhejiang Gongshang University, Stanford University and Fudan University

detail.title: Privatization, Human Capital, and Intergenerational Mobility: Long-term Evidence from China
detail.abstract: This paper examines the long-term impact of privatization on the next generation's education, labor market outcomes, and intergenerational mobility. We study the 1997-2000 privatization of state-owned enterprises (SOEs) in urban China, which displaced more than 35 million workers. Using a triple-differences design that exploits variation in reform intensity across regions, children's birth cohorts, and parents' pre-reform employment status, we find that the reform reduced human capital accumulation and worsened long-run labor-market outcomes for the second generation. These adverse effects operate primarily through intergenerational transmission via parental layoffs, while rising returns to education during the reform period acted as a countervailing force. Furthermore, we show that the reform weakened intergenerational income persistence, which we attribute to the erosion of network-based job search following the reform.

detail.title: Supplemental Light Quality, Control, And CO2 Strategies Impact Strawberry Yield and Quality

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: Funding for this research was received from the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority under project GLASE (greenhouse lighting and systems engineering).

detail.abstract: Horticultural light-emitting diodes (LEDs) enable improved energy efficiency and control relative to conventional high-pressure sodium (HPS) lighting. Carbon dioxide (CO2) enrichment also increases plant biomass and yield for several high-value horticultural crops. This study evaluated greenhouse strawberries using a Cornell University-developed lighting control algorithm, light and shade system implementation (LASSI), which controls light and shade curtains to target a consistent daily light integral (DLI). The first experiment compared supplemental LED lighting with near real-time dimming (10-min intervals) to a target PPFD (RT-LASSI) to conventional HPS lighting treatments with on/off control (LASSI) without CO2 supplementation. The second experiment compared strawberry yield and quality using LED lighting with RT-LASSI combined with CO2 enrichment (CO2-RT-LASSI) to a conventional HPS lighting treatment with on/off control (LASSI). In the first experiment, strawberry cultivars 'Albion' and 'Cabrillo' were grown in a climate-controlled glass greenhouse with a target DLI of 20 mol m-2 d-1. Both the LED and HPS treatments were successful in reaching the target DLI, but the LED treatment received approximately 0.32 mol m-2 s-1 or 2% less PAR relative to the HPS treatment. The LED RT-LASSI 'Albion' treatment resulted in statistically similar marketable fresh fruit biomass with generally equal fruit quality (Brix and titratable acidity) compared to the control 'Albion' treatment (LASSI). The LED RT-LASSI 'Cabrillo' treatment also had statistically similar but a numerically 5% greater fresh fruit biomass with generally equal fruit quality compared to the control 'Cabrillo' treatment. The second experiment only used 'Albion' and added CO2 enrichment to the RT-LASSI treatment to achieve the same target virtual DLI as the HPS control. Because the experiment was conducted in late spring, the average CO2 concentration in the CO2-RT-LASSI treatment was 555 µmol mol-1. CO2-RT-LASSI treatment had 29% greater fruit yield plant-1 , even with an 11% lower DLI than their HPS LASSI counterparts. However, HPS LASSI resulted in a 9% Brix content increase, suggesting a potential trade-off between fruit yield and sweetness. CO2-RT-LASSI provided about 41% energy savings (33% from LED energy efficiency and 8% based on reduced lighting needs from CO2 enrichment). More research is required to replicate findings and better understand the impact of the light spectrum and control strategy on strawberry yield and quality.

title: Non-GAAP Reporting in the Banking Industry: Determinants and Usefulness
affiliations: University of Zurich and PwC Switzerland

detail.title: Non-GAAP Reporting in the Banking Industry: Determinants and Usefulness
detail.abstract: We present the first comprehensive overview of the prevalence, the determinants, and the usefulness of banks' non-GAAP disclosures. Analyzing press releases for a large sample of US banks between 2003 and 2022, we find that banks prefer to disclose industry-specific non-GAAP performance metrics based on ROE instead of non-GAAP earnings. We also show that banks prevalently report non-GAAP capital metrics. Banks disclose non-GAAP performance metrics primarily to inform about their performance when corresponding GAAP metrics are less informative. Banks disclose non-GAAP capital metrics when they experience a weaker capital base, more regulatory attention and low GAAP capital informativeness. Even though industry-specific non-GAAP performance measures are widely reported, we find that banks' non-GAAP earnings are more useful than industry-specific performance measures to predict future bank performance. However, our results also suggest that banks potentially obfuscate lower-quality non-GAAP earnings by disclosing multiple non-GAAP performance metrics. The findings of our empirical analyses reveal unique characteristics of banks' non-GAAP reporting environment that are relevant to users of banks' financial information.

detail.abstract:
Italian abstract: Tra il 2019 e il 2024 l’economia italiana ha registrato una crescita del PIL superiore alla media dell’area dell’euro e a quella del precedente quinquennio. L’espansione è stata trainata soprattutto dal settore privato, dove il valore aggiunto è aumentato di quasi il 10 per cento, beneficiando in larga parte di un generoso stimolo fiscale. Ha riguardato soprattutto le costruzioni e i servizi, mentre la manifattura ha rallentato. La crescita è stata trainata dall’espansione dell’occupazione, a fronte di una dinamica più debole della produttività del lavoro, in calo negli ultimi due anni. Nel tessuto produttivo si registrano l’aumento della dimensione media delle imprese (che resta inferiore alla media dell’area), nonché della loro redditività e propensione ad investire. La produttività d’impresa è stata sostenuta da processi riallocativi e di crescita interna, dalle multinazionali e dalla dinamicità di quelle alla frontiera dell’efficienza produttiva. È, tuttavia, aumentato il divario tra le imprese migliori e il resto del tessuto produttivo. Per colmare il ritardo di produttività rispetto ai principali paesi europei, e a fronte dei recenti segnali di indebolimento, il tessuto produttivo dovrà rafforzarsi in maniera più diffusa e sarà cruciale promuovere una più ampia adozione di tecnologie avanzate.

English abstract: Between 2019 and 2024, the Italian economy recorded GDP growth that exceeded both the euro-area average and that of the previous five-year period. The expansion was mainly driven by the private sector, where value added increased by nearly 10 per cent, largely benefiting from a generous fiscal stimulus. Growth was concentrated in construction and services, while manufacturing slowed. It was fuelled by rising employment, while labour productivity declined over the past two years. The productive system saw an increase in the average firm size (which remains below the euro-area average), as well as in profitability and investment propensity. Firm-level productivity was supported by reallocation and internal growth processes, by multinational companies, and by the dynamism of firms at the productivity frontier. However, the gap between the most efficient firms and the rest of the productive system widened. To close the productivity gap with major European countries – and in light of recent signs of weakening – the production system will need to be strengthened more broadly, and fostering a wider adoption of advanced technologies will be crucial.

title: Financial Leverage in Private Equity Acquisitions: Debt as a Strategic Driver of Governance and Value Creation

detail.title: Financial Leverage in Private Equity Acquisitions: Debt as a Strategic Driver of Governance and Value Creation
detail.abstract:
Private Equity (PE) acquisitions have become a central mechanism for value creation in contemporary corporate finance. Among the tools at the disposal of PE firms, financial leverage plays a pivotal role, not merely as a source of funding but as a strategic instrument that influences both governance structures and operational performance.

Leverage Buyouts (LBOs) typically employ a combination of equity and substantial debt, allowing firms to acquire companies while amplifying potential returns on investment.

The use of leverage introduces a dual effect: it imposes financial discipline on management, incentivizing efficiency and cash flow generation, while simultaneously affecting governance through covenants, incentive schemes, and contractual protections such as drag-alone or tag-alone rights. Furthermore, leverage can drive value creation, whether by enhancing operational performance in well-performing targets or by enabling complex turnarounds in distressed companies.

This paper explores the strategic role of leverage in PE acquisitions by examining both theoretical frameworks and practical implications. Through selected case studies, it illustrates how the structuring of debt influences managerial decision-making, operational improvements, and ultimately, investor returns. By bridging academic concepts with real-world applications, the paper highlights the multifaceted impact of leverage beyond its financial function, positioning it as a critical tool for strategic management and value maximization in private equity transactions.

title: Patient or Pushing? New Institutional Ownership and the Shareholder-Value Orientation of European Non-Financial Firms

detail.title: Patient or Pushing? New Institutional Ownership and the Shareholder-Value Orientation of European Non-Financial Firms

declarations.funderStatement: Parts of this project have been funded by the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft (DFG, German Research Foundation) under Germany's Excellence Strategy – EXC 2126/1– 390838866

detail.abstract: Can we identify a systematic correlation between the emergence of new institutional investors concomitant processes of corporate financialization? Shedding light on this issue this paper contributes to the burgeoning literature on the new political economy of the firm in the era of global finance. Conceptually it develops a framework that links the formation of Asset Manager Capitalism – a new corporate governance regime coined by the re-concentration of ownership – to corporate financialization – a multidimensional process affecting the generation and distribution of profits within and outside the firm. Empirically, the paper applies different econometric estimation techniques to a novel and unique panel of 1,472 firms from 31 European countries and 8 economic sectors over the 2010-19 decade. The results show robust, yet ambiguous and surprising associations between Big Three and Sovereign Wealth Fund shareholdings and corporate financialization that deserve further attention. While the acquisition of financial assets by highly leveraged corporations seems to have come to a hold, new institutional ownership correlates with a stronger shareholder value orientation. Future research might investigate further the necessary context factors and potential causal mechanisms behind these variegated trends.

title: The Pitfalls of Continuous Heavy-Tailed Distributions in High-Frequency Data Analysis
affiliations: University of Economics, Prague

detail.title: The Pitfalls of Continuous Heavy-Tailed Distributions in High-Frequency Data Analysis
detail.abstract: We address the challenges of modeling high-frequency integer price changes in financial markets using continuous distributions, particularly the Student's t-distribution. We demonstrate that traditional GARCH models, which rely on continuous distributions, are ill-suited for high-frequency data due to the discreteness of price changes. We propose a modification to the maximum likelihood estimation procedure that accounts for the discrete nature of observations while still using continuous distributions. Our approach involves modeling the log-likelihood in terms of intervals corresponding to the rounding of continuous price changes to the nearest integer. The findings highlight the importance of adjusting for discreteness in volatility analysis and provide a framework for incroporating any continuous distribution for modeling high-frequency prices.

title: House Price Responses to Monetary Policy Surprises: Evidence from the U.S. Listings Data

detail.title: House Price Responses to Monetary Policy Surprises: Evidence from the U.S. Listings Data
detail.abstract:
This paper presents direct evidence of the immediate causal impact of interest rates on U.S. house prices. Using detailed microdata on daily house listings from 2001 to
2019 and high-frequency monetary policy shocks, the analysis reveals three findings: (1) House prices react within weeks, significantly faster than previously thought. (2)
These effects are primarily driven by surprises to medium- and long-term interest rates. (3) The magnitude of house price responses is comparable to that of stock prices
on announcement days. These findings offer crucial insights for central bankers to more precisely gauge policy effects and mitigate housing market imbalances.

title: What Makes a Paper Seminal? Evidence from 80 Years of Economic Research
affiliations: Frankfurt School of Finance & Management and University of Cape Town

detail.title: What Makes a Paper Seminal? Evidence from 80 Years of Economic Research
detail.abstract: We study what makes an economics paper seminal, using 29,823 articles published in a Top-5 economics journal between 1940 and 2020. Seminal papers are in the Top-1% of within-year citations 16-20 years after publication and continue to accumulate citations, while citations to early hit papers peak 1-5 years after publication. Author prolificness strongly predicts seminality, whereas seniority does not. Co-author network centralities do not predict seminality, although they predict papers' broader influence. Conditional on being Top-5 publication, affiliation rank is not a reliable predictor of seminality and is weakly favorable to lower-ranked affiliations. Combinatorial novelty is insignificant or negatively correlated with seminality, while semantic novelty of abstracts is uninformative. Figures correlate with seminality, whereas tables mainly predict broad influence in the "empirical era." Authors with one additional seminal paper are 1.76 pp more likely to eventually become Nobel laureates.

detail.abstract: We investigate the theoretical mechanisms through which labor turnover adversely affects bank risk and performance. Using monthly matched employer-employee data from Brazil during 2003-2019, we find banks with higher labor turnover show lower risk buffers, higher loan growth, and lower profitability. These adverse effects align with the firm-specific human capital theory. Consistent with our identifying assumptions, the effects are stronger when turnover reduces experience and expertise, among loan officers, as well as across cities and banks. Placebo tests and further analyses confirm our results. The evidence suggests that high labor turnover impairs bank information production, increasing risk and lowering performance.

title: Modulating a neural marker of outcome valence as a function of intention: Feedback-related negativity (FRN) reduction when wins are treated as losses
affiliations: University of Alberta and University of Alberta

detail.title: Modulating a neural marker of outcome valence as a function of intention: Feedback-related negativity (FRN) reduction when wins are treated as losses
detail.abstract: Losses are known to negatively affect decision-making, leading to inflexible and predictable behaviours, when the intention is to win as much as possible (win-maximization). This study aims to explore whether outcome valence can be reconfigured at both the behavioural and neurophysiological levels with a reversed goal state: to lose as much as possible (loss-maximization). Participants (n = 39) were asked to play a binary-response paradigm against an exploitable opponent while their electroencephalogram (EEG) was recorded. For one half of the experiment, participants were asked to win as much as possible, while for the other half, they were asked to lose as much as possible. Participants exhibited comparable degrees of shift and stay behaviours across the given goals, demonstrating flexible and symmetrical behavioural reconfiguration. At the neurophysiological level, FRN amplitudes to wins decreased during loss-maximization relative to win-maximization, while the amplitudes to losses remained comparable. These results emphasize the asymmetrical effects of wins and losses at a neurophysiological level, compared to the symmetrical decision-making at the behavioural level.

title: Should the United States Give People Money? Evidence from High-Quality Empirical Research on Unconditional Cash Transfers

detail.title: Should the United States Give People Money? Evidence from High-Quality Empirical Research on Unconditional Cash Transfers

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I performed data analytic work for Baby's First Years randomized controlled trial in 2022. However, the views expressed here are my own independent assessment of the publicly available research.

contentType.other: Forthcoming publication in the Kansas Journal of Law & Public Policy

detail.abstract:
Unconditional cash is a popular tool for people of all political stripes, forming the basis of policy proposals like Universal Basic Income and an expanded Child Tax Credit. Many rationales for unconditional cash exist. Some defend the policy on efficiency grounds, with arguments that cash is preferable to in-kind support, that it would generate greater economic benefits than costs, or even that it would pay for itself. Others argue for unconditional cash on moral grounds, saying that it would improve recipients' lives, reduce poverty, and lead to a more egalitarian society.

Over the past decade, researchers have conducted multiple high-quality studies to assess the effects of transfers of up to $12,000 in yearly unconditional cash lasting several years. This essay surveys this latest round of research to determine which policy rationales for unconditional cash transfers it supports-if any. It finds that the research supports the moral arguments for unconditional cash transfers more strongly than the efficiency arguments, but that uncertainties remain regarding unconditional cash's long-term effects.

title: The Neoliberal Era Thus Far: An Appraisal
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Neoliberal Era Thus Far: An Appraisal
detail.abstract: This note offers a brief summation of the record of neoliberal policymaking--its principal objects, the extent to which it achieved its object, and furthermore the extent to which in doing so it realized the hopes held and promises made for it. Where all this is concerned the author specifically identifies the "practical" side of the neoliberal project with the rollback of the "industrial development-welfare-macroeconomic management state," and holds that the reformers accomplished much of what they endeavored to do on this point. (If they did not "shrink" the state as some envisaged, they did succeed in arresting its formerly rapid growth, and profoundly altered its resourcing and functioning in line with the tenets of neoliberal ideology.) The result saw business gain enormous latitude, and elites benefit significantly from the economic trend, but distinctly failed to realize the promises made for it with regard to the rejuvenation of industry in mature industrial powers, industrialize less developed economies, restore the growth rates of the post-war boom era, and raise popular living standards--a fact which has generated much discontent. However, reflecting the situation elites remain supportive of neoliberal prescriptions, and the associated (privatized, financialized) neoliberal "model," as for the time being opposition to neoliberalism has been ineffectual, with the result that claims of neoliberalism's demise have been "greatly exaggerated."

detail.abstract: In recent decades, most countries are structured on free market or mixed economies. This points to Adam Smith's idea of the invisible hand, that humans are driven by utility maximising. This suggests that individuals pursuing self-interests like profit will unintentionally benefit the overall well-being of society through market mechanisms. detail.abstract: This note, addressing the gap between the long-term, high-risk character of industrial investment and the short-term and low-risk preference of investors, argues that historically only state support has bridged that gap. It also argues that the alternatives to the state taking up the "planning" role in this manner has been to cede it to the private and especially financial sector, with the result typically technological, industrial and economic stagnation (even as the financial sector often booms).

detail.title: Robust Pricing with Limited Demand Information
detail.abstract: How should a firm price its product when facing limited information about the demand curve? We propose the guaranteed profit ratio (GPR)-the minimum ratio of realized profit to ex-post optimal profit across all potential demand curves-as a criterion for evaluating pricing performance. We characterize prices that maximize this ratio and identify the demand curves that attain it, given only coarse demand information. An illustrative example shows that a GPR-optimal price yields higher realized profit than a price maximizing worst-case profit for most curves considered, and the reasoning suggests that this pattern could extend to broader demand environments.

detail.abstract: It is widely recognized in demographic theories that structural constraints, such as the financial costs of child-rearing, future economic uncertainties, and gender inequities, play a central role in shaping individual fertility intentions. However, previous research often examines these factors in isolation, hindering theoretical integration and effective policymaking. By employing a factorial survey experiment across six countries (US, Spain, Sweden, urban China, South Korea, Japan), we integrate five dominant theoretical perspectives into a unified framework, manipulating the degree of each constraint to assess its relative importance in shaping fertility intentions. Our findings indicate that economic factors, particularly the financial burden and uncertainties regarding future economic conditions, are the most critical structural constraints. They are followed by insufficient workplace and intergenerational family support, as well as gender inequity. In contrast, social norms and values related to fertility were found to be the least influential. Moreover, the relative importance of these structural constraints varies by gender and national contexts, reflecting differences in cultural norms, family dynamics, and institutional frameworks. By integrating multiple perspectives into a unified framework, this study underscores the predominant role of economic factors in shaping fertility intentions, even amid broader cultural shifts associated with demographic transitions and individualistic values.

detail.abstract: This article explores the legal framework governing trademark registration, infringement, and enforcement in Nigeria, with a focus on the significance of timely renewal and due diligence clearance before registering a trademark. It highlights how trademarks serve as critical tools for businesses in building brand identity, protecting goodwill, and promoting consumer trust. The paper analyses key provisions of the Nigerian Trademarks Act and related statutes, outlining the requirements for valid registration, duration and infringement, and remedies available for infringement. A detailed case study of Citilink Accesscorp Ltd v MTN Nigeria Communications Plc illustrates modern trademark warfare and the risks of lapses in rights management. Drawing lessons from the dispute, the article underscores the need for proactive IP strategies and cautions against reliance on litigation, given its costs and uncertainties. It concludes with practical recommendations for brand owners seeking to strengthen their trademark portfolios in Nigeria's evolving commercial landscape.

title: Officers at Common Law

detail.title: Officers at Common Law

detail.abstract:
The Framers of the federal Constitution said almost nothing about how subordinate officers would be held accountable. This Article provides one overlooked explanation for this longstanding puzzle. The Constitution was enacted against a well-defined jurisprudence that has largely fallen from view: a law of officers. When using the term “Officer” and its framework of “Duties,” the Constitution invoked a distinctive method of regulating state power, in which officers were personally responsible—and liable—for discharging duties defined by law. The Framers and Ratifiers of the Constitution expected that these common-law rules would fill the gap left by the document’s silence.

This Article weaves together the strands of statutory and common law that constituted and regulated the early American officer. This system of legal organization, drawn from longstanding English and colonial practice, empowered officers to create a decentralized governing apparatus that blurred the line between public and private. Its regime of harsh personal liability and individual empowerment impeded efforts to construct a top-down hierarchy by empowering and encouraging officers to resist orders from their superiors. As Americans developed a bureaucratic state over the nineteenth- and twentieth centuries, judges and lawmakers replaced this officer-based paradigm of governance with a system of administrative law that was more conducive to the modern state.

The legal regime of early American officeholding is inconsistent with many originalist justifications of the “unitary executive theory,” which assert that the Constitution relies on a combination of managerial control and presidential elections to discipline the state. Because the traditional law of officers centered officers’ independent obligations to law rather than to the executive hierarchy, it actively frustrated efforts to construct the command-and-control executive branch that unitarists believe the Constitution requires. The unitarists implicitly impose a theory of the state that developed as the early American law of officers was fading from view.

title: Development and analysis of single stop trip chain travel patterns
affiliations: Imam Mohammad Ibn Saud Islamic University

detail.title: Development and analysis of single stop trip chain travel patterns
detail.abstract: Trip chain patterns are developed from the 1995 NPTS data set according to trip chain definition using a computer program that comprises trip chain building conditions and criteria. The software that is used to develop the program is Statistical Analysis System (SAS). There are five variables (household characteristics) that are selected to be used in analyzing trip chaining in this research. The construction process of trip chaining reveals fourteen different single stop trip chain patterns. The results show that the most frequent single stop trip chain pattern is Home-Work-Home which is designated numerically as "170117". The percent of trip chains of this single work stop trip chain pattern is 12.10% of overall trip chains and 20.34% of total single stop trip chain patterns. The percentages of households that generate different frequencies of single stop trip chain patterns during the day are 75% once, 19% twice, 4% three times, 2% four times, and 1% five times or more. The results show in general that households with two people, two worker, two vehicle, 1 adult, no children, and an income is equal to $60000 and above represent the highest percent of households and trip chains compared to other classes of household characteristics. The ratio of number of trip chains to households is computed. This rate is called trip chain generation rate (TCGR). It is calculated in two different ways in which the calculation is characterized by a trip chain pattern and a certain household characteristic, then the calculations are characterized by a trip pattern, a certain household characteristic, and a trip chain frequency. TCGR is directly proportional to the number of workers within household and the average increasing rate is about 20%. The rate of increase as the class size increases is almost steady for household vehicle, size and income and the average increasing rates are about 8%, 6%, and 2% respectively. The results show that the class of household size has an obvious effect on generating trip chains of the other selected trip chains patterns. The most affected trip chain pattern by household size is Home-Religious activity-Home and the second most affected are Home-Other Social/Recreational-Home and Home-Went out to Eat-Home trip chain patterns. In general, it has been found that with increase of the class of household characteristics, the TCGR increases with different variations in the increasing rates from certain trip chain pattern to another. Generally, the tendency of generating one trip chain per day is decreasing as the class of household characteristics increases while generating more than one trip per day is increasing as the class of household characteristics increases with some variation of the increasing or decreasing rates among trip chain patterns. Household size characteristic is statistically significant correlated to the development of all selected single stop trip chain pattern and it is the most important variable for all trip chain patterns except Home-Work-Home. Finally, all household characteristics are statistically significant correlated to Home-Work-Home and the most important variables are number of workers and number of vehicles within households.

title: When Is AI Advice Good Enough to Travel On? An Uncertainty Reduction Theory-Based Analysis of Informational, Cognitive, and Temporal Uncertainties
affiliations: Chaoyang University of Technology, Chaoyang University of Technology, Chaoyang University of Technology and Chaoyang University of Technology

detail.title: When Is AI Advice Good Enough to Travel On? An Uncertainty Reduction Theory-Based Analysis of Informational, Cognitive, and Temporal Uncertainties
detail.abstract: Generative-AI chatbots promise frictionless trip planning, but travelers often confront dense or outdated answers. Guided by Uncertainty Reduction Theory, this study models how informational, cognitive and temporal uncertainties shape tourists’ trust in ChatGPT and how online-review credibility conditions these effects. Survey evidence shows temporal and informational gaps consistently undermine clarity, whereas cognitive opacity matters little. Travelers restore confidence mainly through iterative clarification with the bot; peer feedback is helpful only when anchored in highly credible reviews, revealing a boundary for social proof. Once uncertainty falls, intentions to visit recommended destinations and to continue using ChatGPT both strengthen, with technology loyalty further amplifying destination appeal. The research extends URT to generative AI by isolating temporal uncertainty and demonstrating that review credibility gates the value of social validation. Practically, it urges designers and destination managers to surface timestamps, evidence prompts and verified reviews, turning AI curiosity into confident, actionable itineraries.

detail.abstract: Why are some states more open to international trade than others? Although existing explanations emphasize the influence of voters as consumers who benefit from lower tariffs, recent research suggests that democracy does not improve policy responsiveness: high consumption goods with greater impact on voter spending have higher tariffs. These findings contradict observations of pro-poor policies implemented by leaders in low-income democracies. I argue that democratic leaders are incentivized to pay attention to voter interest only on salient products. Leveraging the World Bank Consumption Database and a new merging strategy with fine-grained tariff data, I find that high consumption foodstuff, which tend to be politically salient essential goods, receive lower tariffs. This effect is more pronounced in low-income democracies, where the citizenry is more sensitive to the price of foods, increasing their salience. These findings suggest that democratic leaders do care about voter interests, but only on high salience issues.

title: Organization Capital and Corporate Biodiversity Risk: Evidence from China
affiliations: Xiamen University

detail.title: Organization Capital and Corporate Biodiversity Risk: Evidence from China
detail.abstract: We examine whether firms with high organizational capital (OC) exhibit greater corporate biodiversity risk, using a panel of Chinese A-share listed firms from 2009 to 2021. We document a robust and economically meaningful positive association between OC and a firm-level biodiversity exposure index. The effect remains after controlling for firm characteristics and high-dimensional fixed effects, and after addressing endogeneity with multiple identification strategies. We propose two economic channels through which OC affects biodiversity exposure-information environment and green innovation. Consistent with these mechanisms, we find that the positive OC-biodiversity relationship is stronger for firms with superior information environments (greater analyst and media attention, higher disclosure quality, lower asymmetry) and for firms with more intensive green patenting activity. Further cross-sectional analyses show that this effect is concentrated in privately owned firms, in biodiversity-sensitive industries, in provinces with stricter environmental regulation, in more competitive product markets, and among firms with stronger boards and greater financial slack. Our results are robust to alternative model specifications, propensity score matching, instrumental-variable estimators, and the Heckman two-stage model. Overall, the findings highlight OC as a critical internal driver of nature-related risk recognition and disclosure, particularly in an emerging-market setting where biodiversity risk is particularly relevant.

title: Controlling Complex Contagions
affiliations: University of New South Wales (UNSW) and University of Cambridge

detail.title: Controlling Complex Contagions
detail.abstract: Many social and economic behaviors—from the adoption of new technologies or cultural norms, to protest participation—require social reinforcement to spread. That is, agents take an action if and only if enough of their neighbors in a network do so too. These phenomena are called complex contagions. However, deriving comparatives statics in model of these behaviors has proven elusive, which has rendered policy recommendations for network design intractable. We introduce a new approach by analyzing complex contagions on random graphs. This approach unlocks powerful comparative statics that allow for precise policy recommendations. We find that equilibrium behavior jumps discontinuously from zero at a critical cutoff in network connectivity, and exhibits diminishing returns thereafter. Optimal network design reveals a "missing middle" in the designer's optimal choice: network connectivity is either set at the critical cutoff or substantially above it. Finally, we discuss a number of interventions that a principal can use to control complex contagions.

title: LEY 21.521, LA PRESTACIÓN DE SERVICIOS FINANCIEROS FINTECH: EL DESAFIO DE LA COMISIÓN PARA EL MERCADO FINANCIERO PARA REGULARLOS (Act N°21.521/2023, The Provision Of Financial Services In Fintech: The Challenge For The Financial Market Comission To Regulate Them)
